questions.question: What is IAM and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is a global, free AWS security service that controls who can sign in to your AWS account and what they can do once signed in. It solves the problem of securely managing access for multiple team members without sharing the root user credentials, enabling both authentication (identity) and authorization (permissions) at a granular level.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.answer: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' — it verifies your identity through credentials like username/password or MFA. Authorization answers 'What can you do?' — it determines which actions you are permitted to perform on which resources. In IAM: authentication happens at login; authorization is enforced by policies.

questions.question: What is the root user and when should you use it?
questions.answer: The root user is the identity created when an AWS account is first opened, using the account's email and password. It has unrestricted access to all services. You should use it only for account-level tasks (like closing the account, changing the root email, or enabling IAM billing access). For all daily work, use IAM users or roles instead. Always protect root with MFA.

questions.question: What is the Principle of Least Privilege?
questions.answer: The Principle of Least Privilege states that every user or service should be granted only the minimum permissions required to do their job — nothing more. It limits the blast radius of security incidents: if a user's credentials are compromised, the attacker can only access what that user was permitted to access, not everything.

questions.question: What is an IAM Group and how does it help manage permissions?
questions.answer: An IAM Group is a collection of IAM users. Policies attached to a group automatically apply to all members. This makes managing permissions scalable — instead of attaching policies to 50 individual developers, you create a 'Developers' group, attach the policies once, and add/remove users as the team changes. Note: groups cannot be nested — they can only contain users.

questions.question: What is an IAM Role and how does it differ from an IAM User?
questions.answer: An IAM Role is a temporary, assumable identity without permanent credentials. Unlike IAM Users (which are permanent identities tied to people with passwords/access keys), roles are assumed temporarily by AWS services (like EC2 or Lambda), applications, or cross-account users. Roles issue short-lived credentials via STS that automatically expire, making them more secure than static access keys.

questions.question: How does IAM policy evaluation work when there are conflicting Allow and Deny statements?
questions.answer: IAM uses a default-deny model. The evaluation order is: (1) By default, all actions are implicitly denied. (2) An explicit Allow grants access. (3) An explicit Deny always overrides any Allow — it's the final word. If a user is in two groups where one allows S3 and the other denies S3, the Deny wins and the user cannot access S3.

questions.question: What are the three main types of IAM policies?
questions.answer: (1) AWS Managed Policies — pre-built by AWS for common use cases, maintained by AWS, can be attached to multiple identities. (2) Customer Managed Policies — custom policies you create and maintain, reusable across multiple users/groups/roles. (3) Inline Policies — embedded directly into a single user, group, or role; cannot be reused; useful for one-off access requirements.

questions.question: What is MFA and which MFA devices does AWS support?
questions.answer: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) requires a second verification factor beyond your password — typically a time-based one-time code. AWS supports: Virtual MFA devices (apps like Google Authenticator or Authy — most common), Hardware TOTP tokens (physical fobs for high-security environments), FIDO Security Keys (YubiKey — USB/NFC, phishing-resistant), and hardware OTP tokens specifically for root accounts.

questions.question: What are the five AWS Support plans and their key differences?
questions.answer: (1) Basic — free, 7 Trusted Advisor checks, no technical support. (2) Developer — $29+/mo, business hours support, 1 contact. (3) Business — $100+/mo, 24/7 support, all TA checks, 1-hour production-down SLA. (4) Enterprise On-Ramp — $5,500+/mo, pool of TAMs, 30-min critical SLA. (5) Enterprise — $15,000+/mo, dedicated TAM, 15-min critical SLA, Infrastructure Event Management included.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to troubleshoot an IAM permission issue.
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer reported getting 'Access Denied' when trying to upload files to an S3 bucket, despite being in the Developers group. (Task) I needed to identify why their permissions weren't working. (Action) I checked the user's effective permissions using the IAM Policy Simulator. I discovered their user had an explicit Deny policy attached directly (inline) that overrode the group's Allow — an old access restriction left from a previous project. I removed the inline policy. (Result) The developer regained S3 access within 5 minutes, and I documented the incident to prevent future conflicts.

questions.question: Describe how you would set up secure IAM access for a new team of 5 developers joining a project.
questions.answer: (Situation) New development team joining, all needing similar AWS access. (Task) Provision secure, least-privilege access. (Action) Created a 'Developers' IAM Group. Created a Customer Managed Policy granting access only to EC2, CodeDeploy, and CloudWatch — services the developers actually need. Attached the policy to the group. Created individual IAM users for each developer with console access and required password reset at first login. Added all five users to the Developers group. Enabled MFA requirement via IAM policy condition. (Result) Each developer had the right access within 20 minutes, with no shared credentials and full audit trail.

questions.question: How would you secure an EC2 application that needs to read from S3?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 application needs S3 read access, but hardcoding access keys in code is risky. (Task) Provide S3 access without storing credentials. (Action) Created an IAM Role with a policy permitting s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the specific bucket only. Attached the role to the EC2 instance profile. Updated the application to use the default credential chain (which automatically picks up the instance profile). Removed any hardcoded keys from the codebase and rotated the old keys. (Result) The application could access S3 with no credentials stored anywhere. Credentials rotate automatically, eliminating rotation overhead and key exposure risk.

questions.question: A client's production system goes down at 2 AM. They have Business support. What is the expected response time and how do they contact AWS?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production system down, 2 AM, Business support plan. (Task) Understand the SLA and escalation path. (Action) On Business support, the 'production system down' SLA is less than 1 hour. The client should open a Severity 1 support case via the AWS Support Center console, selecting 'Production system down' as the severity. Business support provides 24/7 phone, email, and chat access. (Result) AWS Support should respond within 1 hour. If the issue persists or escalates to a critical business impact, the client might consider upgrading to Enterprise On-Ramp (30-min SLA) or Enterprise (15-min SLA).

questions.question: Trusted Advisor flagged several issues in your account. How do you prioritize which to fix first?
questions.answer: (Situation) Multiple Trusted Advisor recommendations across different categories. (Task) Prioritize remediation. (Action) Started with red (Action Recommended) items in the Security category — public S3 buckets and unrestricted security groups pose immediate risk. Then addressed Service Limits close to threshold to prevent service disruptions. Moved to Fault Tolerance items (single-AZ instances) for resilience. Tackled Cost Optimization (idle resources) next to reduce waste. Yellow (Investigation Recommended) items were scheduled for the next sprint. (Result) Highest-risk issues resolved first; a 30% cost reduction identified from idle resource cleanup.

questions.question: An engineer accidentally deleted all admin IAM users and now no one can log into the AWS console with admin access. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) All admin IAM users deleted — locked out of the AWS console. (Task) Restore admin access. (Action) This is a root-user-only recovery scenario. Log in to the AWS console using the root user credentials (email + password + MFA). Once in, go to IAM and recreate the admin IAM user or group. Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy. This is precisely why the root user exists — as the recovery identity of last resort. (Result) Admin access restored. Post-incident: enabled IAM password policy, set up deletion protection alerts via CloudTrail/CloudWatch.

questions.question: How would you use the Personal Health Dashboard proactively?
questions.answer: (Situation) Running production workloads on AWS, want proactive alerting on issues. (Task) Set up automated monitoring using Personal Health Dashboard. (Action) Integrated AWS Health API with Amazon EventBridge to capture health events. Created EventBridge rules for event types like AWS_EC2_INSTANCE_STORE_DRIVE_PERFORMANCE_DEGRADED and scheduled maintenance notifications. Routed events to an SNS topic that sends alerts to the on-call Slack channel and creates a PagerDuty incident. (Result) The team receives proactive notification of hardware issues, scheduled maintenance, and region events before they impact customers — often with hours of advance warning.

questions.question: Your team is about to launch a major product feature and expects 10x traffic. You're worried about hitting EC2 limits. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Anticipated traffic spike could exceed EC2 instance limits. (Task) Ensure limits won't block scaling. (Action) Reviewed current EC2 instance limits via Service Quotas console. Identified that the current limit for the required instance type was insufficient for the 10x scenario. Submitted a quota increase request with a business justification and the expected launch date. AWS typically responds within 24-48 hours. Also checked Trusted Advisor's Service Limits category to identify any other limits approaching 80% usage. (Result) Limit increased before launch. No scaling issues during the traffic spike.

questions.question: What are the conditions under which an explicit Deny overrides permissions?
questions.answer: An explicit Deny in any policy — whether it's an AWS Managed policy, Customer Managed policy, Inline policy, or even an SCP (Service Control Policy in AWS Organizations) — always takes priority over any Allow. There is no way to override an explicit Deny with an Allow. The only exception is for the root user, who can sometimes bypass SCPs. This is why it's important to carefully design Deny statements — they are absolute.

questions.question: How would you enforce MFA for all IAM users in your organization?
questions.answer: (Situation) Company policy requires MFA for all console logins. (Task) Enforce MFA programmatically. (Action) Created an IAM policy that denies all actions except MFA-related ones (iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice, iam:EnableMFADevice) when MFA is not present — using the condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false. Attached this policy to all users or a group. Now any user who logs in without MFA can only set up MFA — they cannot perform any other action until they do. (Result) 100% MFA compliance enforced by policy, not relying on users to opt in.

questions.question: Design the IAM architecture for a 3-tier web application on AWS.
questions.answer: For a 3-tier app (web, app, database tiers), the IAM design would be: (1) EC2 instances in each tier get IAM Roles (not users) — web tier role has permission to read from S3 for static assets; app tier role can read/write DynamoDB and call SQS; DB tier role can access Secrets Manager for credentials. (2) Developers get IAM Users in a 'Developers' group with deploy permissions only (CodeDeploy, CloudWatch). (3) Operations get an 'Ops' group with broader read access plus EC2 restart capabilities. (4) Automated pipelines (CodePipeline) use a Role with least-privilege deploy access. (5) All roles use resource-level permissions scoped to only the specific ARNs they need. No access keys stored anywhere on EC2.

questions.question: How does AWS evaluate permissions when a user has multiple policies attached — both at the user level and through group membership?
questions.answer: AWS merges all applicable policies (user-level, group-level, and any resource-based policies) and evaluates them together. The evaluation logic: (1) Start with an implicit Deny on everything. (2) Any explicit Allow from any policy grants access. (3) Any explicit Deny from any policy overrides all Allows. In practice: if a user is in 3 groups and has 2 inline policies, AWS combines all of them, and any single Deny wins regardless of how many Allows exist. This is the union-of-permissions model with Deny dominance.

questions.question: Compare IAM Roles with IAM Users from a security perspective. When would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: IAM Users have permanent credentials (passwords, access keys) that must be managed, rotated, and can be leaked. They are appropriate for human users who log into the console or need long-lived CLI access. IAM Roles issue temporary credentials via STS (15 minutes to 12 hours by default) that automatically expire and rotate — no key management required. Use Roles for: EC2/Lambda/ECS service identities, cross-account access, identity federation (SAML/OIDC), and CI/CD pipelines. The security preference is always Roles over Users when possible, because there are no long-term credentials to steal or accidentally expose.

questions.question: What are Service Control Policies (SCPs) and how do they relate to IAM?
questions.answer: SCPs are a feature of AWS Organizations that set the maximum permissions available in an account or OU. They act as a guardrail — even if an IAM policy Allows an action, an SCP can restrict it at the organization level, and that restriction cannot be overridden by any IAM policy (including root in some cases). SCPs don't grant permissions themselves — they only restrict what IAM can grant. Example: an SCP might prevent any account in the 'Dev' OU from launching resources in certain regions, regardless of what IAM policies say.

questions.question: How would you design an IAM strategy for a multi-account AWS organization with 50 teams?
questions.answer: For a multi-account org: (1) Use AWS Organizations with OUs per environment (Dev/Staging/Prod) or per department. (2) Apply SCPs at the OU level for guardrails — prevent deletion of CloudTrail, restrict regions, block risky services. (3) Use a central Identity account with IAM Identity Center (SSO) — users authenticate once and assume roles in target accounts. (4) Each team gets their own AWS account (isolation). (5) Cross-account roles for shared services (logging, security tooling). (6) All automation uses roles, never long-lived keys. (7) Tag-based access control (ABAC) for scalable permission management as teams grow. This eliminates per-user management across 50 accounts while maintaining least privilege.
